system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-06-12 17:45:00 to 2169-06-15 16:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, laryngeal stenosis, and tracheostomy dependence was admitted for post-operative monitoring after a scheduled tracheostomy tube exchange. She underwent flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation and exchange from a fenestrated to an unfenestrated Portex 8 trach tube due to progressive shortness of breath and discomfort. The procedure was uncomplicated, and she tolerated it well. Post-operatively, she developed mild right forearm erythema and swelling at the IV site, which was evaluated with ultrasound and determined to be superficial thrombophlebitis without DVT. Pain was managed with a short course of low-dose oxycodone in addition to her home regimen. She was unable to tolerate a speaking valve due to increased work of breathing. Her respiratory status remained stable, and she was discharged home with instructions to continue her chronic medications and follow up with interventional pulmonology.
problems: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia originating in the perinatal period
Phlebitis and thrombophlebitis of other sites
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve had a sore throat for about three days, and it’s been really hard to swallow—especially liquids. I keep coughing after I eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, shortness of breath, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or trouble breathing. Just this choking feeling when I swallow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And your trach—any secretions or leakage around it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s been dry. I’ve had trouble with swallowing before, but it seemed to be getting better until about two weeks ago when it got worse again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve reviewed your history—tracheobronchomalacia, laryngeal stenosis, and your tracheostomy since infancy. We’ll need to figure out why you’re having this issue now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a swallow study a while back and they didn’t find anything. I’m worried it’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful to know. We’ve already done a chest X-ray, and it looks clear—no pneumonia or blockage. Your labs are normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Doesn’t look like it. The interventional pulmonology team saw you in the ER and didn’t think you needed a bronchoscopy. But we’ve scheduled a speech and swallow evaluation tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I keep avoiding liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, stick to soft foods and thickened liquids. The speech team will give you specific guidance. We also want to do an EGD—just a camera down your esophagus—to make sure there’s no blockage or irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. It’s just to rule out anything we can’t see from the outside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The speech and swallow team evaluated you earlier. How did it go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They had me try different textures. I did better when I covered my trach while swallowing. They said that helps me use my throat muscles better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s a great strategy. They said you handled regular food well with that technique. No signs of aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So why do I feel like I’m choking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They think it’s due to pharyngeal residue—some food or liquid lingering in your throat after swallowing. Covering your trach helps generate more pressure, clearing it better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that actually makes sense. I do feel like something’s stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did the EGD this morning while you were sedated. I just reviewed the report—your esophagus and stomach look completely normal. No strictures, ulcers, or blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s physically wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not structurally, no. Your symptoms—this globus sensation, the feeling of choking—are likely due to how your throat is functioning, especially with your history of airway issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this related to my GERD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Even though you’re on omeprazole and ranitidine, silent reflux can irritate the throat. But the speech team’s strategy should help a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should keep covering my trach when I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the key recommendation. They cleared you for a regular diet as long as you do that. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your vitals are stable, lungs are clear. Just a few mild wheezes, but that’s usual for you. How’s your swallowing today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had soup this morning and covered my trach like they said. No coughing!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Should I keep doing anything special at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep covering your trach when eating, stay on your current meds—especially the reflux ones—and continue your nebulizer treatments for your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my gabapentin for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that as prescribed. And fluoxetine for your mood—important to keep that steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another swallow study?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. But your primary doctor will follow up to make sure you’re maintaining your weight and tolerating food. If symptoms return, we may reconsider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your swallowing has improved, and all tests were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better knowing it’s not something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send instructions to your primary doctor. Keep using the trach-covering technique, take your meds, and come back if you can’t keep food down or start losing weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, laryngeal stenosis, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and tracheostomy dependence was admitted for evaluation of worsening dysphagia and odynophagia. She reported a three-day history of sore throat and difficulty swallowing, with coughing after liquids. Initial workup showed normal labs and a clear chest X-ray. Speech and swallow evaluation revealed improved swallowing with tracheostomy occlusion, and an EGD showed no mechanical obstruction. Her symptoms were attributed to pharyngeal residue, and she was successfully managed with behavioral strategies. She tolerated a regular diet with technique modification, remained stable, and was discharged home with follow-up instructions.
